arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: The government's lawyer argued that broad orders exceed the judicial power Article III grants. He said judges may address only the injury to the party before them. He said the orders invite forum shopping and conflicting judgments.

The challengers' lawyers argued that the orders are proper. One lawyer said the order would make citizenship vary by state, which the Constitution forbids. Another lawyer said the orders maintain a century-old status quo while the case proceeds.

Justice Sotomayor said the order appears to conflict with four Supreme Court precedents on citizenship. She said those precedents treat children as citizens regardless of their parents' status or loyalty.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: President Trump issued an executive order in January 2025 seeking to change who gets citizenship at birth. Several federal judges issued orders that blocked the policy nationwide. The administration asked the Supreme Court to narrow those orders. The case tests how far a single judge's order can reach.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: Lower courts issued preliminary orders that blocked the executive order across the country. The administration asked the Supreme Court to narrow those orders while the case continues. The challengers asked the Court to keep the orders in place.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The administration wants the Supreme Court to narrow the nationwide orders. It argues that judges may order relief only for the people before them. It says these broad orders let plaintiffs win anywhere while the government must win everywhere. It also says the orders encourage forum shopping and rush judges into decisions.

The challengers want the Supreme Court to leave the orders in place. They say the executive order violates the Constitution's citizenship rule. They say every court that reviewed the order found it unlawful. They say the orders protect the challengers from serious harm while the case proceeds.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The administration says the Fourteenth Amendment grants citizenship to children of former slaves, not to people in the country unlawfully or temporarily. It says broad court orders exceed judges' power and disrupt the separation of powers.

The challengers say the order conflicts with the Constitution's text, court precedent, a federal statute, and a century of government practice. They say the orders give complete relief to the people who sued.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Sotomayor questioned whether the government's position would force hundreds of thousands of people to file separate lawsuits. She asked whether the challengers' proposal resembles a class action or a bill of peace. She said the challengers identify a single group and one question: whether citizenship follows birth on U. S. soil.

Justice Thomas asked the government's lawyer about the history of broad court orders. He asked whether past practices support them. Justice Jackson questioned whether the orders really give relief to people outside the case. She said the orders may simply limit what the government can do.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The ruling could reshape how much relief a federal judge can order against the government. It could affect how challenges to federal policies are litigated nationwide. Questions from the justices do not indicate a final outcome.

sections.heading: What the Court decided
paragraphs: In deciding the stay request, the Court treated universal injunctions as broader than federal courts' authority allows. Such injunctions protect people beyond the plaintiffs.
The Court partly stayed the injunctions, limiting them to relief needed for the plaintiffs with standing.
